section.title: Immorality in the Church
section.sectionRationale: Paul turns from the divisions to a scandal that the proud Corinthians have tolerated: a man living with his father's wife, an immorality that even the pagans would not accept. Their boasting in the face of such sin is intolerable. Paul commands the church, gathered in the name of the Lord Jesus, to hand the man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that his spirit may be saved. He grounds the call for purity in the gospel itself: Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, so the church must cleanse out the old leaven and keep the feast in sincerity and truth, judging those inside the church while leaving outsiders to God.
section.thesis: The church must not tolerate flagrant, unrepentant sin in its midst but must lovingly and solemnly discipline it, handing the immoral man over to Satan that his spirit may be saved, because Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed and His people are called to cleanse out the old leaven and live as a new, unleavened batch of sincerity and truth.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the scandal and the sentence, hand him over to Satan that his spirit may be saved; Christ our Passover and the call to cleanse out the old leaven; and the church's duty to judge those inside while leaving outsiders to God.

units.label: The scandal and the sentence
units.note: hand him over to Satan that his spirit may be saved

verses.text: It is actually reported that there is {{porneia|sexual immorality}} among you, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father’s wife.
And you are proud! Shouldn’t you rather have been stricken with grief and have removed from your fellowship the man who did this?
Although I am absent from you in body, I am present with you in spirit, and I have already pronounced judgment on the one who did this, just as if I were present.
When you are assembled in the name of our Lord Jesus and I am with you in spirit, along with the power of the Lord Jesus,
hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord.

units.label: Christ our Passover, cleanse out the leaven
units.note: a little leaven works through the whole batch

verses.text: Your boasting is not good. Do you not know that a little {{zyme|leaven}} works through the whole batch of dough?
{{ekkathairo|Get rid of}} the old leaven, that you may be a new unleavened batch, as you really are. For Christ, our {{pascha|Passover lamb}}, has been sacrificed.
Therefore let us keep the feast, not with the old bread, leavened with malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth.

units.label: Judge those inside the church
units.note: expel the wicked man from among you

verses.text: I wrote you in my letter not to associate with sexually immoral people.
I was not including the sexually immoral of this world, or the greedy and swindlers, or idolaters. In that case you would have to leave this world.

But now I am writing you not to associate with anyone who claims to be a brother but is sexually immoral or greedy, an idolater or a verbal abuser, a drunkard or a swindler. With such a man do not even eat.
What business of mine is it to judge those outside the church? Are you not to judge those inside?
God will judge those outside. “Expel the wicked man from among you.”

porneia.gloss: Sexual immorality of every kind, sexual activity outside the marriage of one man and one woman. Here it names an incestuous union so shocking that even pagan society condemned it. The word covers a broad range of sexual sin and appears repeatedly in 1 Corinthians as a chief mark of the old life that the gospel is meant to leave behind.

zyme.gloss: Leaven or yeast, a small piece of fermented dough kneaded into a new batch to make it rise. It pictures how a hidden influence spreads silently until it permeates the whole. Paul uses it for tolerated sin: a little of it, left unaddressed, works through the entire congregation, which is why the old leaven must be cleaned out.

ekkathairo.gloss: To clean out thoroughly, to purge completely. The image is of scouring a house of every trace of leaven before Passover. Paul commands the church to cleanse out the old leaven of sin so that it may be in practice what it already is in Christ, a new unleavened batch, holy and set apart.

pascha.gloss: The Passover, and the Passover lamb whose blood spared Israel from death in Egypt. Paul declares that Christ is our Passover lamb, already sacrificed. As Israel purged all leaven from their homes at Passover, so the church, redeemed by the blood of the true Lamb, must purge out the old leaven of sin and keep the feast in sincerity and truth.

basic.context: A man in the Corinthian church was sleeping with his father's wife, a scandal even pagans would not stomach, and instead of grieving, the church was proud. Paul is appalled. He tells them that when they gather in the name of the Lord Jesus, they must remove this man, handing him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, with the aim that his spirit may be saved on the last day. He warns that a little tolerated sin spreads like yeast through the whole church. Because Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, the church must clean out the old leaven and live in sincerity and truth. The church is to judge those inside its fellowship, leaving outsiders to God's judgment.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real case treated as a pattern for church discipline. The severity is aimed at restoration, not mere punishment: the goal stated in verse 5 is that his spirit may be saved. The Passover imagery in verses 6 to 8 grounds the ethics in the gospel: because of what Christ has done, the church must become what it already is.
basic.originalLanguages: The sin is porneia, sexual immorality, here of the most flagrant kind. Tolerated sin is zyme, leaven, a little of which works through the whole batch. So Paul commands them to ekkathairo, to clean out completely, the old leaven. The reason is the pascha: Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, so the redeemed people must purge the leaven and keep the feast.
basic.typology: The Passover of Exodus 12 is fulfilled in Christ, the Lamb whose blood delivers His people from death. The purging of all leaven from Israel's homes before Passover is fulfilled in the church's call to purge out sin. And Paul's closing command, expel the wicked man from among you, draws directly on the covenant refrain of Deuteronomy.
basic.christ: Christ is the true Passover lamb, already sacrificed, whose death both redeems the church and grounds its call to holiness. Discipline is exercised in His name and by His power. The whole logic is gospel-shaped: the Lamb has been slain, therefore the people He has purchased must live as the pure, unleavened batch they now are in Him. Even the severest discipline aims at salvation on the Day of the Lord, the day of Christ's return.
basic.god: God is holy and will not have His people trifle with sin, for a little leaven corrupts the whole. He acts through the gathered church and the power of the Lord Jesus. He is the final judge of those outside, and He is merciful, ordering even discipline toward the saving of the sinner's spirit. His holiness and His mercy meet in the cross of the Passover Lamb.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 12 gives the Passover lamb and the removal of leaven. Deuteronomy repeatedly commands Israel to purge the evil from among them. Matthew 18 lays out the steps of church discipline aimed at winning the brother. Galatians 5 warns that a little leaven leavens the whole lump.
basic.oneStory: From Egypt God redeemed a people by the blood of the lamb and called them to be holy, purging out all leaven. That story reaches its fulfilment in Christ, the true Passover Lamb, whose blood redeems the church and calls it to be a new, unleavened people. Church discipline is part of God's long work of forming a holy people for Himself, a people set apart by the blood of the Lamb until the Day of the Lord.

context.literary:
Chapter 5 begins a new section of the letter. Chapters 1 to 4 answered the report about factions, and from here to the end of chapter 6 Paul deals with problems in the church's moral life, first the case of the man in chapter 5, then lawsuits among believers and sexual immorality in chapter 6. The two chapters are bound by a shared vocabulary of judgment, and by the question of who belongs inside the community and who outside.

The passage falls into three parts. Verses 1 to 5 state the case and pass the sentence. Verses 6 to 8 give the theological ground, the picture of the leaven and the Passover. Verses 9 to 13 clarify the principle by correcting a misreading of an earlier letter and by drawing the line between inside and outside.

The first sentence is built to shock. The Greek puts the offence first and the condemnation second, and the closing clause, 'A man has his father's wife,' arrives only at the end of the sentence, like a blow after a long wind up. In verse 2 Paul sets 'proud' beside 'grief,' as opposites. The Corinthians' pride is the wrong response to the sin and the grief is the right one. Verse 3 sets absence in body against presence in spirit, and Paul has already judged the case as if he were there.

Verses 6 to 8 turn on a single image. The old leaven, the new batch and the unleavened bread of sincerity are all drawn from the Passover. The command in verse 7 and the invitation in verse 8 are held together by the claim that Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. The ethical appeal is built on the gospel event.

The passage closes by quoting Deuteronomy, 'Expel the wicked man from among you,' verse 13. The command that opened the section, to remove the man, is ended with the same note, and the whole is held together as a short circle. The chapter is framed by the removal of a person and by the Old Testament's own words for it.
context.historical:
Corinth's reputation for sexual licence was proverbial. Greek writers used a verb meaning 'to act like a Corinthian' for loose living, and the city's seaport trade and its many temples gave it a character that outsiders noticed. But Paul says that the case at hand is 'of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans,' verse 1. The union of a man with his father's wife was forbidden in Israel's law, Leviticus 18:8 and Deuteronomy 22:30, with a curse in Deuteronomy 27:20 and the death penalty in Leviticus 20:11, and Roman law also forbade marriage with a stepmother. The woman is described as 'his father's wife,' not as his mother, so she was almost certainly his stepmother. Paul does not mention the woman in the judgment, and many think she was not a member of the church, though the text does not say so. The verb 'has' is in the present tense and suggests an ongoing relationship, not a single act.

Why was the church proud? Paul does not say, but the letter hints at the reasons. Some Corinthians prided themselves on a spiritual knowledge and freedom that, in their minds, placed them above ordinary rules. The slogan 'Everything is permissible for me' appears in 6:12. Others may have been reluctant to act against a man of standing. In a city where a wealthy patron could give a household's support to the church, as Gaius did, Romans 16:23, a man of means might be hard to confront. The church's pride may have been a pride in its own broad mindedness.

The setting of the Passover imagery is also worth noting. Paul says in 16:8 that he plans to stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, which falls fifty days after Passover, and so he may well have been writing at about the time of the spring festival. Whether or not that explains the image, the Corinthian church, which included many Gentiles, was being taught to read the Passover as its own story. Jewish households removed leaven before the feast, and Exodus 12:15 says that anyone who ate leavened bread in the week of the feast was to be cut off from Israel. The discipline of the Passover was community discipline.

The earlier letter in verse 9 is lost to us. Paul refers to it as something the Corinthians had misunderstood, and the correction he gives in verses 10 and 11 is a reminder that the New Testament letters we have are not all that Paul wrote.
context.canonical:
The sin of verse 1 has a long Old Testament background. Leviticus 18:8 forbids sexual relations with a father's wife because 'it would dishonor your father,' and Leviticus 20:11 prescribes death. In Genesis 35:22 Reuben lies with his father's concubine, and Jacob remembers it on his deathbed, Genesis 49:3-4, when Reuben loses the firstborn's place. Amos 2:7 charges that a man and his father go to the same girl. The pattern shows that this was a recognised offence against the family and the covenant.

The command to expel comes from a refrain in Deuteronomy. The BSB footnote on verse 13 lists the passages: 13:5, 17:7, 19:19, 21:21, 22:21, 22:24 and 24:7. In Deuteronomy 17:7 the wording is 'So you must purge the evil from among you.' Each time, the evil is something that threatens the covenant community: idolatry, false witness, rebellion, adultery, kidnapping. The point in Deuteronomy is that the holiness of the people is not a private matter. Paul applies the same principle to the church.

The Passover is described in Exodus 12. The lamb was slaughtered and its blood protected the households, Exodus 12:21-23. All leaven was to be removed, and anyone who ate it was to be cut off from Israel, Exodus 12:15 and 12:19. Later the prophets and the Gospels carry leaven as a figure for pervasive influence, as when Jesus warns of 'the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy,' Luke 12:1. Paul's saying about the little leaven appears again in Galatians 5:9.

The passage looks forward to the New Testament's teaching on discipline. Jesus lays out the steps in Matthew 18:15-17, ending with regarding the one who will not listen as a pagan or tax collector. Paul tells Titus to reject a divisive man after a first and second warning, Titus 3:10, and commands the Thessalonians to keep away from a brother who lives in idleness, 2 Thessalonians 3:6. In 2 Corinthians 2:5-11 and 7:8-13 Paul speaks of a painful matter that was resolved by repentance and forgiveness. Whether that is the same man is disputed, but the pattern shows where discipline is meant to lead. Finally the Lamb reappears at the centre of the New Testament: John the Baptist calls Jesus 'the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29, and Peter says the redeemed were bought with 'the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,' 1 Peter 1:19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes with two aims that have to be held together. The first is to shake the church out of its complacency. They had treated the case as a matter for tolerance, even pride, and Paul wants them to feel what the pagan world would feel. The second is to make them act. He does not do the discipline himself from a distance, though he has judged the case. He tells the church to do it, 'when you are assembled,' verse 4. The community, not the apostle alone, is responsible for its own purity.

He also means them to understand why. The reason is not that the church should be respectable. It is that they are 'a new unleavened batch, as you really are,' verse 7, because Christ the Passover lamb has been sacrificed. The command is built on an identity already given. The Corinthians are asked to become what the gospel has made them.

Paul's correction of the misunderstanding in verses 9 to 13 shows the second half of his purpose. He did not want the church to flee the world or to sit in judgment on outsiders. The church's care is for those who claim the name of Christ, 'those inside,' and the world's judgment belongs to God. The first hearers would have understood that discipline protects the church's witness, protects the sinner from false security, and keeps the gospel from being made a cover for a life that denies it.

Finally the aim is restoration, verse 5. The sentence ends with salvation on the Day of the Lord. Any use of this passage that forgets that clause misreads Paul.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The case in verse 1 is a particular event, described. What follows is prescribed for the church in that situation, and many of its principles are meant to continue. The church is not to tolerate open, unrepentant sin by a person who claims to be a brother. The action is taken by the assembled church. It is aimed at the person's good. And it is limited to those inside the fellowship.

Some features are not clearly prescribed for every case. The phrase 'hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh' is described in terms that Paul, with apostolic authority, applies to this man. Churches have disagreed on how far it can be copied, and it is best read with the rest of the Bible's teaching on discipline, such as Matthew 18 and Galatians 6:1, which speak of gentleness and the hope of winning a brother back. Paul himself, in 2 Corinthians 2, urges the church to forgive and comfort a person who has been disciplined.

The passage also does not command withdrawal from the world. Verse 10 says plainly that Paul did not mean the sexually immoral of this world, or else the Corinthians would have to leave it. Christians are not asked to police outsiders, and the passage forbids the sort of harsh self-righteousness that would turn it into a tool for that. Verse 11, 'With such a man do not even eat,' needs care. It addresses a person who claims to be a brother and persists in a pattern of sin, and it does not apply to casual contact or to the ordinary ties of family and work.

debates.question: What does it mean to hand the man over to Satan 'for the destruction of the flesh'?

views.label: Expulsion from the church
views.case: The church is the sphere of Christ's protection, and outside it is the realm of Satan, as Paul speaks of the world in Ephesians 2:2. To put the man out is to give him up to that realm. 'Flesh' here is the sinful nature, and its destruction is the breaking of his sin through the pain of being cut off.

views.label: Physical suffering or even death
views.case: The word for flesh is the ordinary one for the body, and Paul gives Satan power over the body in a way that echoes Job 2:6, where Satan may strike Job's body but must spare his life. Paul mentions sickness and death as a result of abusing the Lord's Supper in 11:30, and of the thorn in his own flesh, a messenger of Satan, 2 Corinthians 12:7.

views.label: Both together
views.case: Others take the sentence to include expulsion and the affliction that might follow. 1 Timothy 1:20 speaks of two men 'handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme,' which suggests a discipline that teaches.

debates.bearing: All views agree on the goal. The purpose clause says that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord. Even those who think physical affliction is included do not take it as a final condemnation.

debates.question: Is the offender of chapter 5 the same man whose forgiveness is urged in 2 Corinthians 2?

views.label: The same man
views.case: The church acted on Paul's instruction, and 2 Corinthians 2:5-8 speaks of one who caused grief and has been punished by the majority, and who should now be forgiven and comforted lest he be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. This fits an offender who has repented, and it shows the intended outcome of discipline.

views.label: A different person or case
views.case: In 2 Corinthians the offence is described as grieving Paul and the church in a general way, and Paul does not mention immorality there. Some think the offender was someone who had personally wronged Paul or the church.

debates.bearing: The text of 2 Corinthians does not name the offence, so certainty is not possible. If it is the same man, it is a clear picture of discipline doing its work. If not, the teaching of 2 Corinthians still shows how the church should treat a repentant sinner.

debates.question: What does 'do not even eat' forbid in verse 11?

views.label: The Lord's Supper
views.case: The meal of the church is the supreme expression of fellowship, and excluding the man from it is the sharpest form of discipline. The context of a church assembled in the name of the Lord Jesus, verse 4, supports this.

views.label: Shared meals in general
views.case: In the ancient world eating together was a mark of friendship and acceptance. On this reading Paul forbids the social ease of table fellowship with a person who claims the name of Christ but lives in unrepentant sin.

debates.bearing: Both readings treat the meal as a sign of acceptance. The point is that the church must not carry on as though nothing were wrong, since such normal friendliness would tell the man that his way was acceptable.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's repeated word for the offence is porneia, in verse 1, with the related noun pornos, a sexually immoral person, in verses 9, 10 and 11. In 1 Corinthians the word covers a broad range of sexual sin, and the list in verse 11 shows how Paul places it alongside greed, idolatry, abuse and drunkenness. The same list recurs, with changes, in 6:9-10, where Paul says that none of these will inherit the kingdom of God.

The verb for 'has' in verse 1, echo, is in the present tense, and the sense is that the man continues to have her, in an ongoing relationship. The phrase 'his father's wife' uses the ordinary word for wife, gyne, and not the word for mother, which fits the law in Leviticus 18:8.

In verse 2 the two words 'proud' and 'grief' are physioo, the verb of puffing up that Paul uses throughout the letter, as in 4:6, 4:18 and 8:1, and penthos, mourning. The second is the word used for grief at a death, as in Luke 6:25. Paul says the church should have been in mourning, as if someone had died. In a sense someone had.

The sentence in verse 5 is compressed. 'Hand over' is paradidomi, the verb used for delivering a person to a court or an authority. Paul uses it of God's giving up of sinners to their own desires in Romans 1:24, 1:26 and 1:28, and of the Father giving up the Son in Romans 8:32. 'Destruction' is olethros, ruin. The Greek of 'the flesh' is sarx, and the choice between body and sinful nature is part of the debate. The BSB footnote notes that the Byzantine and Received Text add 'the Lord Jesus' at the end of verse 5, while the BSB reads 'the Day of the Lord.'

In verse 6 the word 'boasting' is kauchema, the thing one boasts about, which is the Corinthians' pride in their own state. The saying about leaven uses zymoo, to leaven, and the word 'works through' translates the same verb: the whole batch is leavened. Paul quotes it again in Galatians 5:9. Leaven is not always a bad image. Jesus uses it of the kingdom in Matthew 13:33. What matters here is the one thing the image does, which is to spread.

In verse 7 'Get rid of' is ekkatharate, an aorist imperative with the prefix ek-, which suggests a thorough clearing out. The next clause is built on the pairing 'unleavened batch, as you really are.' The 'as you really are' is a statement in the indicative that supports the imperative. It is the same logic as in Romans 6, where the believer is told to become what he is. 'Passover lamb' is pascha, which in the Greek Exodus names both the feast and the lamb, and 'has been sacrificed' is etythe, from thyo, the verb used for slaughtering the Passover lamb in Exodus 12:21. In verse 8 'let us keep the feast' is a present tense, heortazomen, so the Christian life is a feast that goes on. 'Sincerity' is eilikrineia and 'truth' is aletheia, set against 'malice and wickedness,' kakia and poneria.

Verses 9 and 11 use synanamignymi, 'to associate,' which means literally to mix up together with. Paul uses the same verb in 2 Thessalonians 3:14, 'Do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed,' where shame is the aim, not destruction.

typology.fulfillment: The Passover lamb was chosen, slaughtered at twilight, and its blood marked the doorposts so that judgment passed over the house, Exodus 12:21-23. Paul says in verse 7 that 'Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.' The correspondence is substitution and protection through blood. The escalation is that the lamb is a person, the sacrifice is once for all, and the deliverance is from sin and death, not from Egypt. John the Baptist calls Jesus the Lamb of God, John 1:29, and Peter says the redeemed were bought with the blood of a lamb without blemish, 1 Peter 1:19. The type falls short in that the Passover had to be repeated each year, while Christ's sacrifice does not.

typology.type: The removal of leaven and the new unleavened batch
typology.fulfillment: At the first Passover the Israelites left Egypt in haste with unleavened dough, and the feast of Unleavened Bread that followed required the removal of every trace of leaven from the house for seven days, Exodus 12:15-20. Paul turns this into a picture of the church's life. The old leaven, malice and wickedness, is to be cleared out, and the new batch is to be unleavened with sincerity and truth. The escalation is that the whole life of the believer is the feast, since 'let us keep the feast' is a continuing action. The type is incomplete because the church is still being cleansed, and the final purity awaits the Day.

typology.type: Cutting off from the covenant people
typology.fulfillment: In the law the one who ate leaven during the feast was 'cut off from the congregation of Israel,' Exodus 12:19, and the refrain in Deuteronomy was to purge the evil from among the people. Paul applies the same principle to the church. The correspondence is that holiness is a corporate matter and that the covenant community protects itself. The escalation is that the aim is now explicitly redemptive, 'that his spirit may be saved,' and the community is the new covenant people in Christ. The type falls short in that the Old Testament sentence often meant death, while the church's discipline stops at exclusion and aims at restoration.

typology.type: The church as the true Israel in its holiness
typology.fulfillment: Israel was called a holy nation, Exodus 19:6, and Paul addresses the Corinthian church in the same terms, as those who are sanctified in Christ Jesus, 1:2. His appeal to the Passover treats the church as the people who have come out of Egypt, with the exodus as its founding event. The escalation is that the church is made up of Jews and Gentiles and that its deliverance is through Christ. The type is not exact, since the church is not a nation among nations, but the pattern of redemption followed by a call to holiness is the same.

study.christ:
Paul gives Christ one sentence in this chapter, and it carries the whole argument: 'For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed,' verse 7. The sentence tells us three things. First, it names Christ as the lamb. The Passover lamb was the substitute whose blood meant that death passed over the house. Paul assumes that his readers, many of them Gentiles, already know that story and that Christ's death stands in its place. Second, the verb is in the past, a completed act. The sacrifice does not need to be repeated, and it is not a coming event. Third, the possessive 'our' makes it personal. The lamb was slain for this church.

The sentence also tells us how the gospel creates holiness. The command to clean out the old leaven follows from the statement that the lamb has been sacrificed. In Israel the feast came after deliverance, and the removal of leaven was the response of a delivered people. Paul says the same of the church. Holiness is not a means of earning the lamb's protection but the way of life of those who have received it. This is why he can say 'as you really are,' that is, already unleavened in Christ, before telling them to get rid of the old leaven.

Christ is also the one in whose name and power discipline is carried out. The church assembles 'in the name of our Lord Jesus,' and the power of the Lord Jesus is with it, verse 4. This is not discipline by human authority. In Matthew 18:20 Jesus promises to be present where two or three are gathered in His name, and in Matthew 18:18 He promises that what the church binds on earth will be bound in heaven. The Lord who is present is the one who gave Himself.

The goal of discipline is the Day of the Lord, verse 5, which for Paul is the Day of Christ's coming. The aim is that the man's spirit be saved on that day. The Judge on that day is the same person who died as the lamb, so even the most severe discipline is held within His mercy. 1 Corinthians 11:32 says that when we are judged by the Lord we are being disciplined so that we will not be condemned with the world.

Finally the passage gives a picture of Christ's own holiness. He was the lamb without blemish, 1 Peter 1:19, and He is the source of the church's cleansing. The Corinthians' list in 6:11, 'you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God,' comes just after this chapter and says what He has done for the people whom Paul asks to become what they already are.
study.god:
The passage shows God as holy, and the holiness is not abstract. A little leaven works through the whole batch, and a church that tolerates open sin is in danger. The same note is in the Old Testament, where God's presence among His people makes their holiness a serious matter, Leviticus 10 and Joshua 7, and it continues in this letter, where Paul has just told the Corinthians that they are God's temple and that God destroys those who destroy it, 3:16-17. God does not allow sin among those who bear His name to pass as a private matter.

God is also the one who judges the world. 'God will judge those outside,' verse 13. Paul takes the world's judgment out of the church's hands and puts it into God's. This is both a limit and a comfort. The church is not appointed to police the world, and it need not be anxious about those outside, who will be judged by the one who knows everything. It is a doctrine of divine justice that does not depend on human courts.

God is merciful in His discipline. The sentence of verse 5 ends with salvation. The God who hands a man over is the God who wants him saved. Ezekiel 18:23 asks, 'Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked? declares the Lord GOD. Wouldn't I prefer that he turn from his ways and live?' Paul's discipline is an expression of that heart. And the New Testament tells us that the Lord disciplines those He loves, 1 Corinthians 11:32 and Hebrews 12:6.

The passage shows God's redeeming act as the ground of holiness. God did not tell the Corinthians to be clean so that He might save them. He saved them in Christ, the Passover lamb, and then called them to be clean. His grace comes first and His commands follow. This pattern is basic to the doctrine of God in the Bible. He redeems, and then He gives the law, as at Sinai, where the Ten Commandments begin with the statement that He brought Israel out of Egypt, Exodus 20:2.

The passage also shows that God works through a community. He acts through the church assembled, with the power of the Lord Jesus, verse 4. The presence of God with His gathered people is the authority behind the discipline, and also the limit of it. A church that acts without His presence has nothing to act with.

For worship, the lesson is that the church keeps the feast. Verse 8 makes the whole of Christian life a festival, a joyful keeping of the Passover. Holiness is not a grim burden. It is the way of a people who have been rescued and who now eat the bread of sincerity and truth in the presence of the God who rescued them.

crossReferences.note: 'You must not have sexual relations with your father's wife; it would dishonor your father.' The law that Paul has in mind when he says the offence is intolerable even among pagans. The ban is about the father's honour and the family's order, and Leviticus 20:11 gives the penalty, which shows how seriously Israel took it.

'So you must purge the evil from among you.' One of the passages the BSB footnote lists behind 'Expel the wicked man from among you.' In Deuteronomy the purging is carried out by the community, and the aim is to keep the covenant people holy. Paul applies the principle to the church's own life.

'A man is not to marry his father's wife, so that he will not dishonor his father's marriage bed.' It states the same ban as Leviticus 18:8 in the form of marriage. Together they show that the prohibition belonged to the covenant law, so that the Corinthians could not claim ignorance.

The first day of the feast was to see the leaven removed from the houses, and whoever ate leavened bread through the seven days was to be cut off from Israel. The Passover itself carried a discipline. Paul's image of cleaning out the old leaven comes with the sense that community purity was part of the feast.

The elders of Israel are told to select a lamb for each family and slaughter the Passover lamb. The verb for slaughter is the one Paul uses for Christ in 5:7. Paul's sentence places Christ in the place of the lamb that was slain for each household.

'A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough.' Paul uses the same proverb in a very different crisis, false teaching about circumcision. It shows that the saying was a general one, and that error and sin both spread. The method of dealing with each is to stop the spread.

Jesus' steps for a brother who sins: go privately, then with one or two others, then tell the church, and if he refuses to listen, treat him as a pagan or tax collector. The aim is to win the brother. Paul's case is an instance of the last step, with the church acting together.

Paul writes of a person who caused grief, who has been punished by the majority, and who should now be forgiven and comforted. Whether or not he is the man of 1 Corinthians 5, the passage shows that discipline is meant to end in restoration and that the church must be as ready to forgive as it was to act.

The Corinthians who abused the Lord's Supper were weak and sick, and some had died, and Paul says that being judged by the Lord is a discipline so that they will not be condemned with the world. It shows that the Lord's judgment on believers is fatherly and also gives a clue to what 'destruction of the flesh' might involve.

Hymenaeus and Alexander are handed over to Satan 'to be taught not to blaspheme.' It is the only other place where this expression appears, and it gives the purpose as teaching. Paul's hand over to Satan in 1 Corinthians 5:5 is likewise meant to teach, with salvation as the aim.

The redeemed were bought not with silver or gold but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot. Peter makes the same connection as Paul between the Passover lamb and Christ, and bases a call to holiness on it.

'Do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed.' It uses the same verb as 1 Corinthians 5:9 and 11 for associating, and states the aim of withdrawal as shame leading to change. It shows that Paul's discipline is meant to work on the person's conscience.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a holy God who makes a people to live with Him and a garden where they can. Sin breaks the relationship, and from that point the question is how a holy God can live among a sinful people. Israel's answer, given at the Passover and Sinai, is blood and law: a lamb whose blood shields the household, and a set of boundaries that mark God's people as holy. The leaven is part of that story. The people leave Egypt in haste, and the removal of leaven marks a new beginning.

The rest of the Old Testament shows how hard it was to keep the community clean. The refrain of Deuteronomy, 'purge the evil from among you,' comes back again and again, and the prophets accuse Israel of failing to do it. In the end the people were sent away from the land because the evil had not been purged. The question remains open: how can a people be holy when they carry the leaven in themselves?

Paul's answer, in chapter 5, is that the true Lamb has been sacrificed, and the new batch is already unleavened in Him. The church is the new Israel in the sense that it is the people redeemed by the Lamb's blood and called to holiness. The discipline of this chapter belongs to that story. It is not a mark of a harsh church but of one that takes seriously the holiness of the God who lives among it, and that is protected by His own mercy.

The passage also stands between two outlooks. On the one side are those who think of holiness as withdrawal from the world, and Paul corrects that in verse 10. On the other are those who think that freedom means tolerance of everything, and Paul corrects that in verses 1 to 8. The church is to live in the world and be different from it. In the later part of the Bible, Peter calls the church a holy priesthood and a people for God's own possession, and the book of Revelation pictures a bride who has made herself ready, Revelation 19:7-8.

The end of the story is a city into which nothing impure will ever enter, Revelation 21:27, and a feast, the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. The feast that Paul tells the church to keep in verse 8 is a foretaste of it. The church lives between the Passover and the supper, redeemed and being cleansed, until the Day of the Lord, when its holiness will be complete.

quiz.q: What was so alarming about the Corinthians' response to the immorality among them?

options.text: Instead of grieving and removing the man, they were proud.
options.note: Verse 2 rebukes their pride where there should have been grief and action.

options.text: They grieved but were slow to act.
options.note: There is no grief in view; Paul says they were proud.

options.text: They quietly ignored the situation.
options.note: Worse than ignoring, they were boasting.

options.text: They immediately expelled the man.
options.note: They had not acted; Paul must command the removal.

quiz.q: What is the stated aim of handing the man over to Satan?

options.text: That his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord.
options.note: Verse 5 makes the goal explicitly redemptive.

options.text: To punish him with no thought of restoration.
options.note: Discipline is severe, but its aim is salvation, not mere punishment.

options.text: To protect the church's reputation in the city.
options.note: The concern is holiness and the man's salvation, not public image.

options.text: To condemn him finally and forever.
options.note: The opposite; the goal is that his spirit may be saved.

quiz.q: Why does Paul say a little leaven matters so much?

options.text: Tolerated sin spreads quietly through the whole church.
options.note: Verse 6 warns that a little leaven works through the whole batch.

options.text: Sin is only a problem when it becomes widespread.
options.note: The point is that even a little, left alone, corrupts everything.

options.text: One person's sin never affects the wider church.
options.note: This is exactly what Paul denies with the leaven image.

options.text: Small sins do not really concern God.
options.note: Paul treats the tolerated sin as gravely serious.

quiz.q: How does Paul ground the call to purity in the gospel?

options.text: Christ our Passover lamb has been sacrificed, so cleanse out the old leaven.
options.note: Verse 7 roots the ethic in Christ's finished sacrifice.

options.text: By appealing only to the church's fear of consequences.
options.note: The motive is the cross, not merely fear.

options.text: By pointing to the Corinthians' own good record.
options.note: Their record is the problem; the ground of purity is Christ.

options.text: By arguing that holiness earns salvation.
options.note: Holiness flows from the Lamb already sacrificed, not to earn salvation.

quiz.q: Whom is the church responsible to judge, according to this passage?

options.text: Those inside the church, leaving outsiders to God's judgment.
options.note: Verses 12 and 13 assign inside judgment to the church, outsiders to God.

options.text: Everyone in the surrounding city equally.
options.note: Paul explicitly limits the church's judgment to those inside.

options.text: No one at all, since judging is always wrong.
options.note: Paul commands the church to judge those inside.

options.text: Only the church's leaders, never its members.
options.note: The whole assembly is addressed, not leaders alone.

questions: The Corinthians were proud where they should have grieved. Where might you be treating lightly a sin that ought to grieve you?
Church discipline here aims at saving the sinner, not destroying him. How does that reframe the way you think about confronting sin in the church?
A little leaven works through the whole batch. What small, tolerated compromise in your life or community might be quietly spreading?
Because Christ our Passover has been sacrificed, believers are called to become what they already are. How does the gospel motivate your pursuit of holiness rather than mere rule-keeping?
Paul distinguishes judging those inside the church from judging outsiders. How can you hold real accountability within the church while showing grace to those outside it?
Keeping the feast with sincerity and truth means clearing out malice and wickedness. What old leaven do you most need to let Christ clean out this week?

translationNotes.note: Hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved: the destruction of the flesh means the breaking of sinful indulgence, or bodily affliction, and the explicit aim is his salvation on the last day, not his damnation.
Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed draws on Exodus 12; as Israel removed all leaven at Passover, the church redeemed by the true Lamb must purge out the old leaven of sin.
Expel the wicked man from among you quotes the recurring command of Deuteronomy to purge evil from the covenant community, now applied to the church as God's new-covenant people.
